newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. soyoil stranded in China port as prices soar.
newsitem.headline: U.S. soyoil stranded in China port as prices soar.

text.p: A huge gap between Chinese and international prices of soybean oil could be encouraging Chinese buyers to place orders without the necessary import licences, Far East traders said on Friday.
One ship carrying 20,000 tonnes of U.S. soybean oil has been impounded at a Chinese port because it lacked the proper papers, a trader close to the original sale told Reuters.
While refusing to go into details, he did say a gap of almost $100 per tonne between the domestic Chinese and international prices could be partly to blame.

Crude soybean oil was currently 6,250 yuan ($753) per tonne at Chinese ports, a trader in Shanghai said, compared to the $550 to $570 a tonne for U.S. and South American oil, inclusive of cost and freight (c&f).
"Add about 350 renminbi per tonne refining charges and that brings the price to 6,600 (yuan)," the Shanghai trader said.
"With domestic number two (refined soybean oil) now around 7,200, that's a huge profit and great incentive to bring the stuff in," he said.
Prices released on Thursday by China's National Grains and Oils Information Centre showed soybean oil at 7,300 yuan ($879) a tonne in the far northern province of Jilin.
"So there is incentive to bring it in without licences and hope for the best," said the trader involved with the impounded ship.
The Chinese government in theory issues import licences for soybean oil, as well as a wide range of other commodities.
Soybean oil imported without a licence is subject to import duty of 120 percent and with a licence, 13 percent import duty and 13 percent value-added tax (VAT).
Traders said, however, that of the 1.3 million tonnes of soybean oil imported in 1996, import licences had been issued for only 600,000 tonnes to 700,000 tonnes.
